sentence: Centering and Dot Product Conditions
sentence-category-reason: Section heading indicating the focus of the next steps.

sentence: One may show that any regular tetrahedron (in fact, any “centrally‐symmetric” tetrahedron) inscribed in a sphere that is centered at the origin must have its vertices summing to 0.
sentence-category-reason: Deduces a property of vertices summing to zero for such tetrahedra.

sentence: (In our case the sphere is centered at the origin because its equation is x²+y²+z²=N.
sentence-category-reason: Infers the sphere is centered at the origin from its equation.

sentence: ) Thus we may label the four vertices v₁, v₂, v₃, v₄ ∈ ℤ³ so that
sentence-category-reason: Introduces notation/labels for vertices to satisfy the deduced condition.

sentence-category-reason: States the established vertex-sum equation.

sentence: Also, since all vertices lie on the sphere, we have
sentence-category-reason: Sets up a consequence of lying on the sphere.

sentence: vᵢ · vᵢ = N   for i = 1,2,3,4.
sentence-category-reason: Writes the resulting norm equalities for each vertex.

sentence: For a regular tetrahedron the distance between any two distinct vertices is the same.
sentence-category-reason: States property of equal edge lengths in a regular tetrahedron.

sentence:
In other words, for any i ≠ j,
  |vᵢ – vⱼ|² = L²   (constant).
sentence-category-reason: Formalizes equal edge lengths as an equation.

sentence:
But note that
  |vᵢ – vⱼ|² = vᵢ·vᵢ + vⱼ·vⱼ – 2(vᵢ·vⱼ) = 2N – 2(vᵢ·vⱼ).
sentence-category-reason: Performs an algebraic expansion relating distances and dot products.

sentence: Thus the dot product vᵢ·vⱼ (for i ≠ j) must be independent of i and j.
sentence-category-reason: Concludes that the pairwise dot product must be constant.

sentence: Call that common value c.
sentence-category-reason: Defines a symbol for the common dot product value.

sentence:
That is, for i ≠ j,
  vᵢ·vⱼ = c.
sentence-category-reason: States the constant dot product relation explicitly.

sentence:
In particular, the edge‐squared is
  L² = 2N – 2c.
sentence-category-reason: States and applies the explicit formula for the edge length squared in terms of N and c.

sentence: Finding the Common Off‐Diagonal Dot Product
sentence-category-reason: Announces the goal of the next step (to find the common off-diagonal dot product).

sentence:
Using the fact that the vertices sum to 0 we have
  0 = (v₁ + v₂ + v₃ + v₄)·(v₁ + v₂ + v₃ + v₄)
   = Σᵢ (vᵢ·vᵢ) + 2 Σ_{i<j} vᵢ·vⱼ
   = 4N + 2·6c   (since there are 6 pairs).
sentence-category-reason: Expands the squared sum and computes the expression using dot products and counting pairs.
Solves the obtained equation for c.

sentence:
So for any two distinct vertices we have
  vᵢ · vⱼ = –N/3.
sentence-category-reason: States the deduced common off-diagonal dot product value for distinct vertices.

sentence:
Returning to the edge‐squared we then find
  L² = 2N –2(–N/3) = 2N + 2N/3 = 8N/3.
sentence-category-reason: Substitutes c into the edge-length formula and simplifies.

sentence: Since the tetrahedron is nondegenerate (L > 0) these numbers are positive.
sentence-category-reason: Checks positivity of computed quantities given nondegeneracy (L > 0).

sentence: Integrality Forces N to be a Multiple of 3

sentence: The vertices are in ℤ³ so every dot product vᵢ·vⱼ is an integer.

sentence: In particular the off‐diagonal value –N/3 must be an integer.
sentence-category-reason: Infers that the specific off-diagonal dot product must be an integer.

and

sentence: A Determinant Computation Shows M Must be a Square
sentence-category-reason: Announces the plan: use a determinant computation to constrain M.

sentence:
It is a known fact that if you have three “independent” vectors v, w, x in ℤ³ with
  v² = w² = x² = 3M and v·w = v·x = w·x = –M,
then one may show (by a short computation) that the absolute value of the determinant of the 3×3 matrix A having these vectors as columns is
sentence-category-reason: Sets up the theoretical context and states a known fact relating vectors and the determinant.
States the resulting determinant magnitude formula to be used.

sentence:
(One way to see this is to note that if you write the 3×3 Gram matrix G = AᵀA, then
  G = k · B  with k = M and
   B = [3  –1  –1; –1  3  –1; –1  –1  3].
sentence-category-reason: Explains the method via the Gram matrix and its structure.

sentence: A quick computation shows that det(B) = 16, so det(G) = 16 M³, and hence |det A|² = 16 M³.
sentence-category-reason: Carries out the computation of determinants to justify the stated formula.

sentence: However, since A has integer entries, its determinant must be an integer.
sentence-category-reason: Infers that an integer-entry matrix has integer determinant to set up a number-theoretic condition.

sentence: In other words, 4·M^(3/2) is an integer.
sentence-category-reason: Deduces integrality of 4·M^(3/2) from |det A|, a logical inference without computation.

sentence: This forces M^(3/2) itself to be an integer, so M must be a perfect square.
sentence-category-reason: Concludes M^(3/2) is integer and hence M is a perfect square; a logical deduction.

to have an inscribed regular tetrahedron with vertices having integer coordinates is that N = 3m² (with m a positive integer), and that this condition is also sufficient (since an example exists for every such m).
